hook.text: Two suspects sit in separate rooms. Each must decide: confess or stay silent.

buildup.text: Game theory studies strategic decisions where your outcome depends on others' choices.

discovery.text: John Nash proved every game has at least one equilibrium: a point where no player benefits from changing their strategy.

twist.text: Nash equilibria are often not optimal. Both prisoners confess though both staying silent gives a better joint outcome.

climax.text: Game theory reveals a key truth: rational self-interest can produce collectively irrational outcomes.

punchline.text: Your best move depends on theirs. That is the game.

quiz.question: What did Nash prove about games?
options: The most aggressive player always wins
Every game has at least one equilibrium point
Cooperation is always the optimal strategy

hook.text: Two friends are caught shoplifting. Police separate them. If both stay silent, light sentence.

buildup.text: Each prisoner reasons: if the other stays silent, I gain by confessing. If the other confesses, I must confess too.

discovery.text: The dominant strategy is to defect, but mutual cooperation beats mutual defection.

twist.text: Real humans cooperate more than theory predicts. In experiments, about 40% cooperate even in one-shot games.

climax.text: The Prisoners Dilemma appears everywhere: arms races, climate change, price wars.

punchline.text: The rational choice leads to the worst outcome for both.

quiz.question: Why do both prisoners confess even though silence is collectively better?
options: They want to punish each other
Confessing is individually rational regardless of the other's choice
They cannot understand the payoff structure

hook.text: You must meet a stranger in New York City with no way to communicate. Most people independently choose Grand Central.

buildup.text: Coordination Games and Focal Points sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: Schelling found people use focal points: culturally prominent choices that stand out.

twist.text: Focal points are culturally specific. A Japanese pair might pick Shibuya Crossing.

climax.text: Coordination Games and Focal Points matters because better design changes real decisions.

punchline.text: Without words, we find each other through shared expectations.

quiz.question: What is a focal point in game theory?
options: The optimal mathematical solution to a game
A culturally prominent choice that players independently gravitate toward
The point where both players decide to stop playing

hook.text: A negotiator splits a pie: every slice you get, I lose. But the best negotiators find ways to bake a bigger pie.

buildup.text: Zero-Sum vs Positive-Sum Thinking sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: Most economic interactions are positive-sum. Trade creates value for both sides.

twist.text: Zero-sum bias leads to destructive competition. Companies sabotage rivals instead of growing markets.

climax.text: Before competing, ask: is the pie fixed or can it grow? If it can grow, cooperate first, then divide the larger result.

punchline.text: The best strategy is often making the pie bigger, not fighting over slices.

quiz.question: What is zero-sum bias?
options: Correctly identifying competitive situations
Mistakenly assuming every interaction has a fixed total where one person's gain is another's loss
Always cooperating even in competitive scenarios

hook.text: A soccer kicker who always goes left is easy to stop. Randomizing left and right makes each individual kick harder.

buildup.text: Mixed Strategies and Randomness sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: Walker and Wooders studied tennis serves and found professionals randomize almost exactly as game theory predicts.

twist.text: Humans are bad randomizers. We avoid repeating the same option and create detectable patterns.

climax.text: In competitive situations, notice if you've a pattern. If your opponent can predict you, your strategy leaks value.

punchline.text: Predictability is a gift to your opponent. Vary your play.

quiz.question: Why are humans bad at mixed strategies?
options: They always choose the mathematically optimal option
They avoid repeating choices and create detectable patterns
They lack understanding of probability theory

hook.text: You receive $100 to split with a stranger. You offer $1 and keep $99. The stranger rejects it, and you both get nothing.

buildup.text: In the ultimatum game, one player proposes a split and the other accepts or rejects. Rejection means both get zero.

discovery.text: Rational theory says accept any offer above zero. Experiments show offers below 20% are usually rejected.

twist.text: Offers vary by culture. The Machiguenga in Peru offer about 15%. American students offer about 45%.

climax.text: The ultimatum game proves humans are not pure profit maximizers. We punish unfairness even at personal cost.

punchline.text: We burn money to punish greed. Fairness is that powerful.

quiz.question: Why do people reject low offers in the ultimatum game?
options: They do not understand they will also get nothing
They prefer punishment of unfairness over personal profit
The game rules require rejection of low offers

hook.text: You get $10 to share. The other person must accept whatever you give. No rejection possible. Average gift: $2.80.

buildup.text: The dictator game removes punishment. The receiver can't reject. Standard theory predicts the dictator keeps everything.

discovery.text: Most dictators give something. Social norms, guilt, and intrinsic fairness preferences drive giving even when there's.

twist.text: When dictators are anonymous and believe the receiver can't identify them, giving drops sharply.

climax.text: The Dictator Game matters because better design changes real decisions.

punchline.text: We give partly because someone is watching.

quiz.question: What happens when dictators are made fully anonymous?
options: They give more because guilt increases
Giving drops sharply without accountability
Their behavior does not change

hook.text: A capuchin monkey receives a cucumber slice. She is content. Then she sees her neighbor receive a grape.

buildup.text: Inequity Aversion sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: Inequity Aversion reveals the behavioral mechanism driving the outcome.

twist.text: Advantageous inequity aversion is weaker. People dislike receiving less far more than they dislike receiving more.

climax.text: Inequity aversion shapes salary negotiations, taxes, and redistribution policy.

punchline.text: Fairness matters so much we sacrifice to achieve it.

quiz.question: What did the capuchin monkey experiment reveal?
options: Monkeys prefer grapes to cucumbers for nutritional reasons
Even primates reject unequal treatment, showing inequity aversion
Monkeys cannot understand fairness concepts

hook.text: You watch someone cheat a stranger. You were not harmed. Yet you pay your own money to punish the cheater. Why?

buildup.text: Third-party punishment means bystanders who are unaffected personally still pay to punish norm violators.

discovery.text: Third-Party Punishment reveals the behavioral mechanism driving the outcome.

twist.text: The threat is often enough. Knowing bystanders will punish deters cheating even if punishment rarely happens.

climax.text: Third-party punishment is the foundation of law and social order. We all enforce fairness, not those directly harmed.

punchline.text: We punish cheaters even when we are not the victim. That is society.

quiz.question: Why is third-party punishment important for cooperation?
options: It generates revenue from fines
It deters cheating by showing norm violations will be punished by anyone
It only works in small communities

hook.text: A player earns more than you. You can pay $1 to reduce their earnings by $3. You do it. Both are worse off.

buildup.text: Spiteful behavior reduces another's payoff at a cost to yourself. It's punishment without moral justification, only.

discovery.text: Experiments show people sometimes destroy value to close gaps. Status matters more than absolute wealth for some.

twist.text: Spite decreases with distance and anonymity. You are more spiteful toward those you can see and compare with directly.

climax.text: Recognizing spite in yourself is the first defense. Asking would I pay to hurt them if no one knew?

punchline.text: Spite costs you money to make someone else poorer.

quiz.question: When does spiteful behavior increase?
options: When people are anonymous and far apart
When people can see and directly compare with others
When absolute wealth is high for both parties

hook.text: You send $5 to a stranger. The amount triples to $15. The stranger decides how much to return. Rationally: nothing.

buildup.text: The trust game measures trust via sending money and trustworthiness via returning it.

discovery.text: Berg's experiment showed most people send about half and recipients return about a third.

twist.text: Oxytocin increases trust. Participants given oxytocin nasal spray sent markedly more money.

climax.text: Trust is an economic lubricant. Countries with higher trust levels have higher GDP.

punchline.text: Trust pays off. Not always, but on average, always.

quiz.question: What does the trust game measure?
options: How quickly people make financial decisions
Trust through money sent and trustworthiness through money returned
Whether people prefer gambling over saving

hook.text: A firm pays above minimum wage. Workers are not contractually obligated to work harder. Yet productivity rises 20%. Why?

buildup.text: The gift exchange model: employers offer generous wages as a gift, and employees reciprocate with higher effort.

discovery.text: Akerlof proposed efficiency wages: above-market pay buys loyalty and effort that monitoring alone can't achieve.

twist.text: The gift must feel intentional. Mandated minimum wage increases don't produce the same reciprocity as voluntary.

climax.text: Reciprocity works in both directions. Pay cuts trigger effort reduction disproportionate to the cut.

punchline.text: Pay generously and they work harder. Cut pay and they work less.

quiz.question: Why does above-market pay increase worker effort?
options: Workers fear being fired if they do not reciprocate
Workers feel the generous wage is a gift and reciprocate with effort
It is legally required to work harder when paid more

hook.text: A seller cheats once and earns $100. Word spreads. No one buys from them again.

buildup.text: Repeated games change strategy. When you interact again, today's defection invites tomorrow's punishment.

discovery.text: Axelrod's tournaments proved Tit for Tat wins: cooperate first, then mirror the other's last move.

twist.text: If the game has a known endpoint, cooperation unravels from the end. Knowing the last round, both defect.

climax.text: Reputation is the mechanism. In repeated interactions, your track record is your strategy.

punchline.text: Reputation takes years to build and seconds to lose.

quiz.question: What strategy won Axelrod's repeated game tournaments?
options: Always defect to maximize individual gain
Tit for Tat: cooperate first, then mirror the other's last move
Random choices to remain unpredictable

hook.text: You help a stranger. A different stranger helps you later. You never met, but your reputation traveled ahead of you.

buildup.text: Indirect Reciprocity sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: Nowak showed indirect reciprocity sustains cooperation in large groups where direct repeated interaction is unlikely.

twist.text: Online reviews are an indirect reciprocity system. You review for strangers; strangers review for you.

climax.text: Indirect Reciprocity matters because better design changes real decisions.

punchline.text: Help someone and the help comes back from someone else.

quiz.question: How does indirect reciprocity sustain cooperation?
options: Through legal contracts between strangers
Through reputation networks that reward helpful behavior from third parties
By forcing direct repeated interactions

hook.text: Before the game, one player says: I will cooperate. There's no enforcement. Standard theory says ignore it.

buildup.text: Cheap talk is communication that costs nothing and can't be enforced. Theory says it should be ignored since talk.

discovery.text: Experiments show cheap talk works. Pre-play communication increases cooperation substantially, especially face-to-face.

twist.text: Written promises are weaker than spoken ones. Eye contact and vocal tone carry honesty signals that text can't transmit.

climax.text: Cheap Talk and Promises matters because better design changes real decisions.

punchline.text: Words are cheap. But breaking them is expensive.

quiz.question: Why does cheap talk increase cooperation despite having no enforcement?
options: People always believe what others say
Breaking a promise has social and psychological costs
The game rules change after communication

hook.text: A poker beginner bluffs randomly and loses. After 100 hands, she bluffs selectively and starts winning.

buildup.text: Reinforcement learning: repeat actions that worked, avoid actions that failed. No theory needed.

discovery.text: Trial and Error in Games reveals the behavioral mechanism driving the outcome.

twist.text: Trial and Error in Games shows that intuition alone misreads how people actually choose.

climax.text: Early luck distorts learning. To improve, track why you won, not just that you won. Process matters more than outcome.

punchline.text: Winning by luck teaches nothing. Winning by process teaches everything.

quiz.question: What is the danger of reinforcement learning in games?
options: It always finds the optimal strategy quickly
It can lock into bad strategies if early luck reinforces poor choices
It requires reading complex strategy books

hook.text: After five rounds, your opponent chose left three times. You now believe left is likely. You adjust right.

buildup.text: Belief learning: you form beliefs about what others will do based on their history and best-respond to those beliefs.

discovery.text: Fictitious play is the simplest version: count the opponent's past moves and assume those frequencies will continue.

twist.text: Smart opponents know you're learning and adjust to exploit your beliefs. The learning creates a moving target for both.

climax.text: In strategic settings, the environment learns back. Unlike nature, opponents adapt.

punchline.text: Your opponent is also learning about you. Both models must be mutual.

quiz.question: What makes belief-based learning challenging in strategic settings?
options: Beliefs are always accurate reflections of opponents' strategies
Opponents adapt to exploit your beliefs, creating a moving target
Only one player uses belief-based learning at a time

hook.text: You partly learn from past rewards and partly from thinking about what would have worked.

buildup.text: Colin Camerer's EWA model combines reinforcement learning and belief learning into one framework.

discovery.text: EWA weights each strategy by experience: what it earned and what it would have earned if chosen.

twist.text: Newcomers lean on reinforcement. Experienced players lean on beliefs.

climax.text: EWA predicts behavior better than either learning model alone. We're neither pure trial-and-error nor pure calculators.

punchline.text: We learn from what happened and what could have happened.

quiz.question: What does the EWA model combine?
options: Emotions and rational analysis
Reinforcement learning and belief-based learning
Individual preferences and group behavior

hook.text: A new restaurant opens. Nobody comes. Then one table fills. Suddenly a queue forms.

buildup.text: Social learning means copying successful others instead of experimenting yourself.

discovery.text: Imitation is efficient in stable environments. Copy the best performer and skip costly exploration.

twist.text: If everyone imitates, nobody explores. The group gets stuck on early winners that may not be the best option.

climax.text: Balance imitation with experimentation. Copy others to start, but test new options to avoid following a crowd.

punchline.text: Copying saves time. But if everyone copies, nobody leads.

quiz.question: What is the risk if everyone uses imitation learning?
options: The group converges on the best possible strategy
Nobody explores, so the group gets stuck on early and possibly suboptimal winners
Individual creativity increases through collaboration

hook.text: A coin lands heads three times. You bet heads next. But the coin is fair. Three flips are not enough data.

buildup.text: Over-Fitting to Small Samples sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: Over-Fitting to Small Samples reveals the behavioral mechanism driving the outcome.

twist.text: Experts over-fit too. Fund managers with three years of good returns are treated as geniuses.

climax.text: Before changing strategy based on recent events, ask: is this a real pattern or a small sample?

punchline.text: Three data points are a coincidence, not a conclusion.

quiz.question: What is over-fitting in strategic decision-making?
options: Using too much data to make decisions
Treating random patterns in small samples as meaningful signals
Perfectly matching strategy to the game environment

hook.text: Pick a number from 0–100. The winner is closest to two-thirds of the average.

buildup.text: Level-0 players pick randomly. Level-1 players best-respond to random. Level-2 players best-respond to level-1.

discovery.text: Nagel's beauty contest experiment showed average guesses around 33, consistent with 1-2 steps of thinking, not infinite.

twist.text: Thinking too many steps ahead can backfire. If you play at level 5 but others play at level 1, you overshoot and lose.

climax.text: Level-K Thinking matters because better design changes real decisions.

punchline.text: The best strategy depends on how deeply others think.

quiz.question: Why can thinking too many levels ahead backfire?
options: Deeper thinking always finds the optimal solution
Your strategy overshoots if opponents think fewer steps
More thinking levels means more cooperation

hook.text: Cognitive Hierarchy Theory: a simple choice shows how real behavior departs from strict rationality.

buildup.text: Camerer's cognitive hierarchy model assumes a distribution of thinking levels.

discovery.text: The model fits data better than Nash equilibrium in one-shot games. People don't assume others are perfectly rational.

twist.text: The distribution is Poisson-shaped with an average around 1.5 steps. Very few people think beyond level 3.

climax.text: In negotiations, estimate your opponent's thinking level. Match it and go one step further.

punchline.text: Think one step deeper than your opponent. No more, no less.

quiz.question: What does cognitive hierarchy theory assume about players?
options: All players think at the same level of depth
Players have different thinking depths and best-respond to lower levels
Only the smartest player can win any game

hook.text: A player picks the better option 70% of the time, not 100%. They know which is better but occasionally choose the worse.

buildup.text: Quantal Response Equilibrium sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: McKelvey and Palfrey showed QRE explains data better than Nash in many games.

twist.text: As stakes increase, behavior gets closer to Nash. Higher payoffs motivate more careful thinking.

climax.text: QRE teaches a practical lesson: expect opponents to make mistakes, and plan for error, both theirs and yours.

punchline.text: We choose well most of the time. But not all of the time.

quiz.question: What does QRE suggest about decision-making?
options: People always choose the mathematically optimal option
Better options are chosen more often but noise causes occasional errors
People choose randomly regardless of payoffs

hook.text: A chess computer evaluates millions of moves. A grandmaster evaluates ten.

buildup.text: Satisficing in Strategic Settings sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: Satisficing in Strategic Settings reveals the behavioral mechanism driving the outcome.

twist.text: Satisficing in Strategic Settings shows that intuition alone misreads how people actually choose.

climax.text: Know when to optimize and when to satisfice. High stakes with clear information: optimize.

punchline.text: Good enough, chosen quickly, beats perfect, chosen too late.

quiz.question: When does satisficing outperform optimization?
options: When there is unlimited time and perfect information
In uncertain environments where the cost of finding the optimum is very high
Satisficing never outperforms optimization

hook.text: A poker player watches six opponents, the pot, the cards, and a TV screen.

buildup.text: Attention is limited. In complex games, players can't track all relevant information, so they focus on salient cues.

discovery.text: Gabaix showed that limited attention explains pricing anomalies. If consumers can't process all product attributes.

twist.text: Attention as a Scarce Resource shows that intuition alone misreads how people actually choose.

climax.text: Simplify your decisions. When overwhelmed, focus on the 2 or 3 most important factors.

punchline.text: You cannot watch everything. Choose what to watch wisely.

quiz.question: How can opponents exploit limited attention?
options: By simplifying their strategies for transparency
By creating complexity that overloads decision-making
By reducing the number of choices available

hook.text: A painting estimated at $5,000 sells for $22,000 at auction. The winner regrets it the next morning.

buildup.text: Auction fever is the emotional escalation that occurs during competitive bidding.

discovery.text: The winner's curse: the winning bidder likely overestimates the item's value.

twist.text: eBay's countdown timer amplifies fever. Sniping in the last seconds triggers panic bidding from those who thought they.

climax.text: Set a maximum bid before the auction starts. Write it down. When the fever hits, stick to the number.

punchline.text: If winning feels thrilling, you probably overpaid.

quiz.question: What is the winner's curse in auctions?
options: The winner gets the item at an unfairly low price
The winner likely overestimated the item's value by beating all others
The auction house takes an excessive commission

hook.text: Bargaining and Fairness Norms: a simple choice shows how real behavior departs from strict rationality.

buildup.text: Bargaining theory predicts quick efficient outcomes. Real negotiations stall because both sides use different fairness.

discovery.text: Babcock found self-serving bias in fairness: each side selects evidence supporting their preferred outcome.

twist.text: Strikes and lawsuits often cost more than the disputed amount. The fight is about principle, not profit.

climax.text: In negotiations, understand the other side's fairness frame. Resolving the frame conflict often resolves.

punchline.text: Negotiations stall on principle, not on dollars.

quiz.question: What is self-serving bias in negotiations?
options: Deliberately cheating the other party
Each side genuinely believing their preferred outcome is the fair one
Always accepting the other party's first offer

hook.text: You prefer candidate A but vote for B because only B can beat C, whom you dislike most.

buildup.text: Strategic Voting sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: Gibbard and Satterthwaite proved no voting system is immune to strategic manipulation.

twist.text: Polls enable strategic voting by revealing who can win. Without polls, voters express true preferences more often.

climax.text: Voting systems shape strategy. Ranked-choice reduces strategic voting by letting you express a true first choice safely.

punchline.text: Every voting system can be gamed. The best ones make gaming unnecessary.

quiz.question: What did the Gibbard-Satterthwaite theorem prove?
options: Some voting systems are perfectly fair
No voting system is completely immune to strategic manipulation
Strategic voting always produces the best outcomes

hook.text: Two children fight over a cake. A parent says: one cuts, the other chooses. Both get fair slices.

buildup.text: Mechanism Design Basics sets up the incentives, biases, and tradeoffs driving the choice.

discovery.text: Vickrey's second-price auction makes honest bidding optimal. You bid your true value because you only pay.

twist.text: Good mechanisms make cooperation the selfish choice. Like traffic lights, the rule aligns individual incentives.

climax.text: When behavior is bad, ask: is the mechanism wrong? Changing the rules often works better than trying to change people.

punchline.text: Don't fix the players. Fix the rules.

quiz.question: What makes Vickrey's second-price auction effective?
options: It ensures the lowest bidder always wins
Honest bidding is the optimal strategy because winners pay the second-highest price
It eliminates all competition between bidders

hook.text: Spectrum auctions raised $60 billion in the US. The rules were designed using behavioral game theory.

buildup.text: Behavioral game theory blends classical strategy with psychology. It accepts that players are strategic but imperfect.

discovery.text: Applications range from kidney exchange programs to carbon permit markets.

twist.text: Behavioral Game Theory in Practice shows that intuition alone misreads how people actually choose.

climax.text: The future of policy design uses behavioral game theory: rules that work for imperfect, biased, emotional humans.

punchline.text: Design for real humans, not theoretical models.

quiz.question: How does behavioral game theory differ from classical game theory?
options: It ignores strategic thinking entirely
It accepts that players are strategic but imperfect and emotional
It only applies to simple games with two players
